name: The Lord's manifestations (vibhūti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's own divine manifestations, by which he stands pervading the worlds (10.16). Asked in which beings and states he is to be contemplated (10.17), he names the principal ones — the self in all beings, then the chief of each class (10.20–39) — says there is no end to them and that the list is only an indication (10.19, 10.40), gives the rule that whatever is glorious or mighty springs from a portion of his splendour (10.41), and ends that he supports the whole world with a single portion (10.42). Whoever knows his vibhūti and yoga in truth is joined with unwavering yoga (10.7).

members: the self seated in all beings; the beginning, middle and end of beings (10.20)
Viṣṇu among the Ādityas; the radiant sun among lights; Marīci among the Maruts; the moon among the lunar mansions (10.21)
the Sāmaveda among the Vedas; Vāsava (Indra) among the gods; manas among the faculties; sentience (cetanā) in beings (10.22)
Śaṅkara among the Rudras; the lord of wealth among yakṣas and rākṣasas; fire (Pāvaka) among the Vasus; Meru among peaks (10.23)
Bṛhaspati among household priests; Skanda among generals; the ocean among waters (10.24)
Bhṛgu among great seers; the one syllable among utterances; the sacrifice of japa among sacrifices; the Himālaya among immovable things (10.25)
the aśvattha among trees; Nārada among divine seers; Citraratha among gandharvas; the sage Kapila among the perfected (10.26)
Uccaiḥśravas among horses; Airāvata among lordly elephants; the king among men (10.27)
the thunderbolt among weapons; the wish-yielding cow among cows; Kandarpa the begetter; Vāsuki among serpents (10.28)
Ananta among nāgas; Varuṇa among water-dwellers; Aryaman among the ancestors; Yama among restrainers (10.29)
Prahlāda among daityas; time among those that reckon; the lord of beasts among beasts; Vainateya among birds (10.30)
the wind among purifiers; Rāma among weapon-bearers; the makara among water-creatures; Jāhnavī among rivers (10.31)
the beginning, middle and end of creations; knowledge of the self among sciences; vāda among debaters (10.32)
the letter a among letters; the dvandva among compounds; imperishable time; the ordainer facing every way (10.33)
all-seizing death; the arising of what is to be; fame, fortune, speech, memory, retentive intelligence, steadfastness and forbearance among the feminine (10.34)
the Bṛhat-sāman among sāmans; the gāyatrī among metres; Mārgaśīrṣa among months; the flower-bearing season among seasons (10.35)
gambling among deceivers; the splendour of the splendid; victory; resolve; the sattva of those who have it (10.36)
Vāsudeva among the Vṛṣṇis; Dhanañjaya among the Pāṇḍavas; Vyāsa among sages; Uśanas among seer-poets (10.37)
the rod among subduers; policy among those who seek victory; silence among secrets; the knowledge of knowers (10.38)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's sovereign form (rūpam aiśvaram), which Arjuna asks to see (11.3–4) and which, since his own eye cannot see it, he sees with a divine eye given by the Lord (11.8): the whole world, divided in many ways, standing as one in the god's body (11.7, 11.13), with countless mouths, eyes and arms, without beginning, middle or end, as bright as a thousand suns (11.10–19); then fierce, the worlds and the warriors of both sides entering its flaming mouths (11.20–30), declared by the Lord to be Time (11.32). Shown by grace through the Lord's own yoga (11.47), not attainable by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerity (11.48, 11.53), but by undivided devotion (11.54).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord is unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world (10.3); the beginning of the gods and great seers, whose origin they do not know (10.2); from him alone arise all the states of beings (10.4–5), and the seven great seers and the Manus were born from his mind (10.6); he is the origin of all, from whom everything proceeds (10.8), the seed of all beings without whom nothing moving or unmoving could exist (10.39); he stands supporting the whole world with a single portion (10.42); he alone knows himself by himself (10.15); Arjuna praises him as father, object of worship and weightiest teacher of the world, with none equal (11.43), who pervades all and is therefore all (11.40).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: To those ever yoked who worship him with love the Lord gives the yoga of understanding (10.10) and, out of compassion, abiding in their own being, destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.11); Arjuna's delusion is gone through the word spoken out of favour to him (11.1); the Lord gives the divine eye (11.8) and, being gracious (prasanna), shows the supreme form by his own yoga (11.47); Arjuna prays 'be gracious' (11.25, 11.31, 11.45) and seeks his grace (11.44); for those whose awareness (cetas) is set on him the Lord becomes before long the deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra (12.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Knowing the Lord as the origin of all, the wise worship him, their thought on him, awakening one another and speaking of him, content and delighting (10.8–9); by undivided devotion alone he can be known, seen and entered in truth (11.54); whoever does his work, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being comes to him (11.55); those who fix their mind on him and worship him with supreme faith are 'the most yoked' (12.2); the devotee dear to him bears the marks of 12.13–19, and those who follow the teaching with faith are exceedingly dear (12.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: In praise Arjuna calls the Lord the imperishable, the supreme to be known (11.18), and 'the imperishable — being and non-being, and what is beyond' (11.37). In ch. 12 'the imperishable, the unmanifest' is the object of a second kind of worship, described as indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable and constant; its worshippers also reach the Lord, but their hardship is greater, for the unmanifest goal is hard for the embodied (12.1–5).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna acknowledges Kṛṣṇa as the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier, the eternal divine Person, as all the seers declare (10.12–13).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Because Arjuna cannot see the Lord with his own eye, the Lord gives him a divine eye with which to behold his sovereign yoga (11.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The worshippers of the imperishable are even in understanding everywhere (samabuddhi) (12.4); the devotee dear to the Lord is the same in pain and pleasure (12.13), toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, blame and praise (12.18–19).

name: The paths of the Gītā: action, knowledge, meditation and devotion

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Ch. 12 offers, by capacity, fixing mind and understanding on the Lord (12.8), the yoga of practice (12.9), work for the Lord (12.10) and relinquishing the fruit of all actions (12.11); it then ranks knowledge above practice, meditation above knowledge and relinquishing the fruit of actions above meditation, peace following on relinquishment (12.12).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord says: 'of those that reckon I am time' (10.30), 'I alone am imperishable time' (10.33), and, answering 'who are you?', 'I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds' (11.32).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: In the fierce form the warriors of both sides rush into the Lord's flaming mouths like rivers into the ocean and moths into a fire (11.26–30); asked who he is, the Lord answers 'I am Time, grown mighty, maker of the destruction of the worlds, engaged here in drawing in the worlds'; even without Arjuna the opposing warriors will not survive (11.32).

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'I am the self seated in the resting-place (āśaya) of all beings' (10.20); abiding in his devotees' own being, the Lord destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.11).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'Of utterances I am the one syllable (ekam akṣaram)' (10.25) — the syllable the Gītā names oṃ at 8.13.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna calls the Lord the imperishable, 'being and non-being (sad asat), and what is beyond them' — or, on another construal, the imperishable beyond being and non-being (11.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord says: 'I am the self (ātman) seated in the resting-place of all beings' (10.20).

name: Being merely the instrument (nimitta-mātra)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: After declaring himself Time, the destroyer of worlds, the Lord tells Arjuna that the opposing warriors have already been struck down by him; Arjuna is to rise, win glory and be 'merely the instrument' (nimitta-mātra); he is to slay Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa and the others 'already slain by me', and not be distressed (11.32–34).

notes: Compare cpt:god-as-true-agent (a later school's formulation). The Gītā passage does not itself discuss the relation of this to the agent's responsibility.

name: The marks of the devotee dear to the Lord (BhG 12.13–20)

names.name: yo madbhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ ('who is my devotee, he is dear to me')

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The devotee dear to the Lord hates no being, is friendly and compassionate, without 'mine' and without the sense of 'I', the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing, ever content, a yogin, self-restrained, firm in resolve, with mind and understanding offered to the Lord (12.13–14); neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation (12.15); without expectation, pure, capable, impartial, rid of distress, relinquishing every undertaking (12.16); neither rejoices nor hates, grieves nor craves, relinquishing good and evil (12.17); the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free of attachment, the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady in judgement (12.18–19). Each group ends with 'he is dear to me'; those who with faith follow this 'nectar of dharma' are exceedingly dear (12.20).

members: mayy arpitamanobuddhi (mind and understanding offered to the Lord)
not disturbing and not disturbed by the world
free of harṣa, amarṣa, bhaya, udvega (elation, intolerance, fear, agitation)
neither rejoicing, hating, grieving nor craving
same toward enemy and friend, honour and dishonour
same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain
notes: Several marks recur in the Gītā's other portraits: nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ (2.71), na dveṣṭi (2.57, 5.3), na śocati na kāṅkṣati (18.54), mānāpamāna / mitrāri / sarvārambhaparityāgī / tulyanindā... (14.24–25), śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu tathā mānāpamānayoḥ (6.7).
